top.line: Five agent readers make long articles easier to consume
top.para: The articles are deep and long, so rather than shorten them, five agent readers go through each after it is written: a Librarian, a Cartographer, a Historian, an Explainer and a Storyteller. On five agent behaviour policy articles they catalogued 662 items, flagged 32 problems, mapped 45 concepts and produced nine maps and five decks.

s0.line: Prose first, then five readers extract views from it
s0.para: The article stays the source and no reader adds a claim: two readers build a graph, three write short views. The run checked 662 anchors verbatim and flagged 32 problems, acting as fact-checkers unasked. New concepts across the five fell 17, 11, 5, 11, 1, and each article now opens with Read it another way.

s1.line: Writing finds the argument, so the graph comes after
s1.para: Generating an article from a graph does not work, because writing is how a journalist discovers the narrative, as Liquid content needs water said. That article also imagined a historian and a librarian for each story, and projections checked against one graph. This applies the idea to the site's own articles without changing how they are written.

s2.line: Two readers build the graph, three write for people
s2.para: The roles come from the SG/Send agent team. The Librarian catalogues every item with its source sentence; the Cartographer, merged with the ontologist, builds three altitudes and maps. The Historian writes under 400 words, the Explainer under 250, and the Storyteller a deck of 6 to 9 slides.

s3.line: Seven agent runs read five articles in parallel
s3.para: Five articles on agent behaviour policies, from 7 to 10 October, were read by agents each given one role file. Five Librarians ran in parallel using 403,000 tokens, the Cartographer took 14 minutes and 264,000 tokens, and every output was checked against its format by script.

s4.line: Cataloguing every sentence turned the Librarian into a fact-checker
s4.para: All 662 anchors were found verbatim, with 161 claims against 40 items presented as evidence. Told to flag, not fix, the Librarian raised 32 flags: a 17.8 million total that should be about 14.2 million, a twelve-item list with ten, an unsupported military attribution, content only in images. Corrections will follow separately.

s5.line: The Cartographer merged five names for one method
s5.para: It built 13 classes, 24 verbs, 45 concepts and 78 edges at site, topic and article altitude. It merged hope with expectation, second reader with maker-checker, and found one method under five names, moving a rule to a stronger barrier, while keeping reach and blast radius apart. Its 37 feedback items await a second pass.

s6.para: The Historian picked a quoted nugget per article and found the set moved from vocabulary to configuration; Re-anchoring introduced one concept and reused 25. Its unnamed pattern: the rule moves out of the agent, and each article stops one barrier short. It also spotted that new meant new to the set, not the site.

s7.line: Two-minute explanations and code-drawn decks for phones
s7.para: The Explainer writes for a small-business owner: the point, an example, why it matters, one line to remember, defined terms. The Storyteller writes decks as data in nine layouts, rendered at 1080 by 1350 for LinkedIn. Image-model prompts are ready in the vault but unrun, lacking an API key.

s8.line: Each article now opens with Read it another way
s8.para: Under the abstract, In two minutes is open by default, with the arc, pictures, map and catalogue a click away; it works without JavaScript and in the markdown twins. The Article Views vault holds role files, catalogues, ontology, maps, decks and checks, and opens as an app.

s9.line: The views check articles against themselves, not the world
s9.para: Truth of cited facts remains the Journalist's job. Scripts check anchors, edges, limits and quotes, but a subtly unfair summary passes, so the author reads each view. New is relative without the site altitude, the feedback round trip is unapplied, and the run cost about 1.1 million tokens.

s10.line: Next: desk roles, the round trip, a site ontology
s10.para: The readers join the Historian on the newsroom desk so every new article gets views. The Librarian's second pass and the flagged corrections follow, a site-wide ontology makes new mean new, and one deck goes through an image model with its cost counted. The articles stay long.
